science.title: Preliminary evaluation of a qPCR HRM assay for differentiation of Leishmania major and Leishmania tropica
science.description: Rapid and accurate identification of Leishmania species is important for the diagnosis and epidemiological surveillance of cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL). High-resolution melting (HRM) analysis has emerged as a rapid molecular approach for species discrimination. This study aimed to preliminarily evaluate a quantitative real-time PCR coupled with HRM (qPCR-HRM) assay targeting kinetoplast minicircle DNA (kDNA) for differentiation of Leishmania major and Leishmania tropica in northeastern Iran. A qPCR-HRM assay targeting the kDNA region was developed using species-specific primers. Clinical samples from 60 patients with suspected CL in North Khorasan and Razavi Khorasan provinces were examined microscopically and cultured. DNA extracted from cultured promastigotes was analyzed using qPCR-HRM, and the results were compared with conventional PCR and ITS1-rDNA sequencing. In addition, ITS1-rDNA sequence analysis was performed to evaluate the genetic diversity of L. major isolates. Among the 60 suspected CL samples, 13 were positive by molecular analysis. qPCR-HRM successfully differentiated reference strains of L. major and L. tropica based on distinct melting temperature profiles, with a mean ΔTm of approximately 0.86 °C (L. major: 84.13 °C; L. tropica: 83.27 °C). All clinical isolates were identified as L. major by qPCR-HRM and confirmed by ITS1 sequencing, showing complete agreement between the two methods. ITS1-rDNA analysis of the 13 L. major isolates identified nine sequence types and seven haplotypes. The qPCR-HRM assay demonstrated promising performance for rapid differentiation of L. major and L. tropica under the conditions evaluated in this study. However, further validation using larger numbers of direct clinical specimens representing both species is required before routine diagnostic application.

science.title: ABLIM1 supports cerebrovascular endothelial barrier integrity in an IL-1β-treated hCMEC/D3 model
science.description: In Alzheimer’s disease (AD), the role of Actin-binding LIM protein 1 (ABLIM1), which is highly enriched in the brain endothelium, in blood-brain barrier (BBB) dysfunction remains unclear. Our integrative multi-omics analysis, integrating single-cell transcriptomics from AD patient cerebrovascular endothelial cells, transcriptomics from animal models, and vascular endothelial proteomics, identified ABLIM1 as the only overlapping gene across three datasets. We used an inflammatory cell model by treating human cerebral microvascular endothelial cells (hCMEC/D3) with interleukin-1β (IL-1β), which significantly decreased transendothelial electrical resistance (TEER) and markedly reduced ABLIM1 mRNA expression. Furthermore, we identified transcript variants 15 and 16 as the predominant ABLIM1 isoforms in hCMEC/D3 cells. These variants share identical coding sequences and encode the same protein. Lentiviral-mediated knockdown of ABLIM1 significantly impaired barrier integrity, as shown by the reduced TEER, while ABLIM1 overexpression effectively attenuated the IL-1β-induced TEER decrease. Collectively, our findings suggest that ABLIM1 supports cerebrovascular endothelial barrier integrity in an IL-1β-induced inflammatory model, highlighting its potential as a candidate for further investigation in BBB modulation.

science.title: Transcriptomic profiling of inner ear hair cell spontaneous regeneration reveals the key role of dlx5a
science.description: Sensory hair cells (HCs) are susceptible to damage, typically causing permanent hearing and balance deficits in mammals due to limited regeneration. Understanding spontaneous regeneration in non-mammalian models offers key insights for restoring sensory function. Here, we establish a zebrafish semicircular canal crista HC injury model and characterize subsequent regeneration and functional recovery processes. Lineage tracing demonstrates that regenerated crista HCs derive from preexisting and newly formed supporting cells (SCs) that emerged after crista HC injury via both mitotic and non-mitotic mechanisms. Single-cell transcriptomic sequencing of otic vesicles across a regeneration timeline reveals that transcriptomic dynamics peak at 24 h post-injury and uncovers a coordinated multicellular response, including activated inflammatory signaling in immune cells and regenerative pathways in SC populations. Finally, we identify dlx5a as a key transcription factor required for crista HC regeneration. In this work, we provide a framework for understanding vestibular HC regeneration that may inform regenerative therapies for sensory restoration. This study establishes a zebrafish inner ear hair cell injury model, characterizes hair cell regeneration at cellular and single-cell transcriptomic levels, and identifies dlx5a as a key regulator of spontaneous regeneration.

science.title: Recursive introversion, iterative extroversion and transitive ambiversion
science.description: This study proposes a theoretical formalization of personality dynamics in which introversion, extroversion, and ambiversion are modeled as recursion, iteration, and transitivity, respectively. Rather than treating these phenomena as fixed traits, the article interprets them as interacting processual regimes unfolding within a nonlinear and multilayered system. The model is grounded in complex systems theory, nonlinear dynamics, and a formal vocabulary designed to describe the interplay between internal reprocessing, external responsiveness, and adaptive integration. The contribution of the article is conceptual and formal rather than empirical. To prevent the formal model from remaining entirely detached from observable data, the article also includes a small exploratory empirical anchoring based on an anonymous survey. This provides indirect but nonconfirmatory support for the operational distinction between recursive, iterative, and transitive personality-process indicators. It derives analytical expressions for the interaction of internal and external factors and clarifies the interpretive role of key parameters, including sensitivity coefficients, weighting factors of stimuli, and synergy parameters. These quantities are introduced as structural and context-sensitive variables, not as fixed psychological constants. Accordingly, the present work does not claim psychometric validation, direct diagnostic readiness, or established forecasting power. Its significance lies in offering a mathematically explicit framework that may guide future empirical testing, simulation studies, and domain-specific operationalization in psychology, education, organizational research, and related fields. Formalization provides a path toward quantitative personality research while remaining fully aware of its present limits. It provides a theoretical basis for further interdisciplinary work at the intersection of psychology, the cognitive sciences, systems theory, and computational modeling. In this sense, the proposed framework should be understood not as a finished applied instrument but as a first formal language within which future research may investigate behavioral archetypes, regime transitions, and algorithmic approximations of differentiated information-processing styles in human and artificial agents.

science.title: Digital exclusion and health in older adults: a systematic review
science.description: Healthcare systems are turning increasingly digital. Digital exclusion restricts access to a wider range of health-related resources among older adults, which delays prevention and treatment, posing additional health challenges. The study aims to systematically review the published evidence on digital exclusion and its implications for health outcomes among older adults. We conducted a systematic review following PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO#CRD420250655824), searching five databases and major institutional sources up to March 2025 to identify studies linking digital exclusion to health outcomes in adults aged ≥60, with explicit consideration of socioeconomic determinants. Our findings indicate that digital exclusion among older adults is associated with the convergence of socioeconomic disadvantage, health-related vulnerabilities, and contextual barriers across three levels of the digital divide. These contribute to a poorer quality of life and adverse health outcomes in later life. Digital exclusion is therefore not merely a technological challenge, but a manifestation of structural inequities that requires coordinated, system-level responses, including affordable access, digital skills support, age-friendly service design, and non-digital alternatives for those who remain excluded.
